title: Thérèse in the dark
hookLine: in her last darkness, Thérèse pulls up a chair beside those who can't believe
last: LOVE IN THE HEART OF THE CHURCH.

lines: A SEAT AT A STRANGE TABLE.
cards: A sheet of paper, folded small, tucked inside a little book of the Gospels. Tradition says Thérèse of Lisieux copied the Creed onto it and kept it close in her last illness.
Why would a nun whose whole life was prayer carry the Creed like a note in a pocket? Because in her last months, believing had stopped feeling like anything at all. She called it darkness.
And she gave it a strange address, a place where she'd been seated. Today, the table of sinners.

teach.h: THE THOUGHT OF HEAVEN GOES DARK.
teach.b: First, the darkness. In the last part of her notebooks, written for her prioress, Thérèse says the thought of heaven, once so sweet to her, went dark. She writes of a thick fog.
When she tried to rest her heart there, the darkness seemed to mock her. She kept praying, and kept her duties. Second, the surprise.
Before this, she admits, she could hardly believe there were people with no faith at all. She assumed they spoke against what they really thought.
Now she understood that some might honestly see nothing, and the darkness taught her to take them seriously. Third, the table. She calls those who cannot believe her brothers.

teach.h: SEATED AT THEIR TABLE, AS FAMILY.
teach.b: She says she is seated at their table, eating the bread of sorrow with them, and won't ask to get up until the Lord says so. From that chair she prays for everyone there, asking mercy for us, not for them.

It echoes the man at the back of the temple in Jesus's parable, who prays, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." Some readers say this one page changes how they hear the rest of her book.
The Little Flower knew the dark from the inside. She didn't lecture the people at that table. She sat down.

teach.h: I DO BELIEVE, LORD: HELP MY UNBELIEF.
teach.b: And she held on to a cry that belongs to anyone in that chair, from a father in Mark's Gospel with a sick son: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief."

how: Catholics read Thérèse's account of her trial of faith in Story of a Soul, and some ask her prayers for people who struggle to believe, or pray for them in her spirit.

games.q: what does “the table of sinners” mean?
o: the place in church kept for public penitents in Lent
Thérèse's image for sitting with those who can't believe
a convent meal where nuns confess their faults aloud

games.q: the table of sinners — tap the pairs.
p: what she ate at their table

s: Thérèse's last months were full of sweet feelings of faith
she wrote of a thick fog over the thought of heaven, and kept praying anyway.
she called those who could not believe her brothers
and said she was seated at their table, praying mercy for everyone there.
she always understood people who had no faith
she admits she once assumed they spoke against what they really thought. the darkness changed that.

games.q: you're Thérèse. the thought of heaven, once so sweet, has gone dark, and believing feels like nothing. what do you do?
o: stop praying until the feeling comes back.
stay seated at the table with those who can't believe, and pray for everyone there.
announce to the whole convent that your faith is gone.
games.why: she kept praying and kept her duties, and stayed at the table of sinners, asking mercy for us, not for them.

practice: Bring to mind one person for whom faith is closed, painful, or simply not there: a friend, a parent, a child, maybe a corner of yourself.

Don't argue or plan a speech; pull up a chair beside them, as Thérèse did, and share the quiet. If you pray, say for both of you the father's words, help my unbelief; if you don't, keep them company in your mind, with respect.
If the dark ever feels like not wanting to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The table of sinners. Thérèse's image for her last darkness: seated beside those who can't believe, sharing their bread, and praying for everyone at the table. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: unbelief, the word in the father's cry in Mark, help my unbelief.

carryVoice: Your line: faith is held, not felt. Thérèse kept her seat beside the ones who can't believe, and kept praying. See you tomorrow.
